prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms confined at the magic wavelength allow time to be measured at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the first round, the novelty objection is the one that matters, and I think it can be answered in the citation itself. The 2005 prize gave us the comb that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize gave us control of single trapped quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. Neither contains the lattice idea: Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil, so that thousands of atoms are interrogated at once and the stability and systematics are fundamentally better than for a single ion. That is a different way of building a clock, not only a better one. As an instrument builder I judge a technique by whether it was calibrated, intercompared and reproduced, and this one has been: RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others run lattice clocks that agree at the 10^-18 level over fibre links. It has already enabled millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, relativistic geodesy and sharper limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings. Five of eight members prefer it, and the two-name credit is the most compact on the shortlist, leaving room under the three-person ceiling.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that a sceptic can still read lattice clocks as the best continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes rather than a discovery about nature. Danielsson and Lindroth set a higher bar of surprise, and I cannot say they are wrong to do so. The attribution is also a judgment: Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made real contributions to the early Sr and Yb demonstrations, and Ye's records rest on comb and laser-stabilisation work and a large JILA team. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I do not regard that as required, but if the committee thinks it is needed, then B008 is the better choice today, not B023.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 and argues that the Z2 classification is a different discovery from the 2016 topological-phase prize. He and Kroll also raised testing a B035 plus B008 pairing.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between the Z2 classification and the integer quantum Hall and Thouless-Haldane lineage, so I do not treat 2016 as disqualifying B008. My test for B008 is the same one I apply to B035: a consistent standard of adjacency, and on that standard B035 is not worse off than B008. On the pairing, I do not support it. B008 would need Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and B035 Katori and Ye, which is five people against a ceiling of three. Dropping to a trimmed trio would force an arbitrary choice from two achievements with different credit structures. I would rather the committee settle one achievement cleanly. I would still rely on you and Mehlig to say whether the Molenkamp credit can be worded around the experiment alone.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B008 because a simple general mechanism, the Z2 invariant, was predicted first and then confirmed in HgTe, and notes that six members placed it in their top three with the same trio.
responses.response: The agreement on the trio is real, and I take your point that theory first and experiment second is the pattern the prize has honoured most reliably. But agreement on three names does not settle whether those three names are the right ones. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the specific HgTe system that Molenkamp measured, and Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Roy carried the idea to three dimensions, with Hasan's ARPES as the observational test. A citation around the Kane-Mele prediction and the HgTe observation is defensible, but it is a judgment that leaves out people whose work the experiment depended on. For B035 the omissions are smaller and sit at the margins of the claim. That difference in how much credit is left outside the names is why I stay with B035, while keeping B008 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B035, but applies a standard of surprise about nature, and her work on atomic structure is close to the magic-wavelength physics that underlies the lattice clock.
responses.response: You are the member best placed to judge the magic-wavelength condition, so I take your caution seriously. I would answer your surprise standard this way: the discovery was that a many-atom lattice can be made free of the first-order perturbations that were assumed to limit any neutral-atom clock, and that is a statement about nature that was not obvious beforehand. I would write the citation around that idea. Please say in the final round whether the magic-wavelength condition, as an atomic-structure result, matches what you think the citation should highlight. I also note your closeness to the physics and would ask that it is recorded, as you did, with no tie to Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B023 because IceCube found something nature had not told us, and holds B035 to be chiefly a gain in precision. He accepts the attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is not airtight.
responses.response: I ranked B023 first in my own opening and I still think the diffuse flux is a real discovery that I would be glad to see recognised. I disagree that clocks are only a gain in precision. A clock at 10^-18 sees the gravitational redshift across a millimetre, and that gives new tests of fundamental physics that no earlier clock could make. On B023 my position is unchanged from round 1: the attribution among a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND outside the trio, is something I cannot verify, and the associations with TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are still moderate in significance. I do not think B023 should be decided this year without an expert report on the AMANDA-to-IceCube design history, which the Chair can request.

responses.point: Kroll supports B035, thinks the redefinition of the second is not required, and discloses a loose link to the Hall/JILA environment through his doctoral year in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: We agree on the merits and on the redefinition: the prize should reward the invention and its demonstration, not wait for a metrology committee. Your disclosure is noted and I do not think it requires you to step back, since you report no collaboration with Ye or Katori. I would add one request. Since you are the member closest to the precision-measurement community, can you tell us whether any priority question between Katori's Sr lattice and the early Yb or Sr work at JILA, SYRTE and PTB would make you want the credit wording changed? If an expert report can settle that, I think it would remove the strongest attribution objection and keep the two-name configuration safe.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges optical lattice clocks to be a distinct invention after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or a refinement. This is the central open question, and it is a matter of weight rather than fact.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd or the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups have priority claims strong enough to change the two-name credit. I cannot settle early Sr and Yb dates from the record we have.

Whether the B008 attribution, with BHZ and the three-dimensional generalisation left outside the trio, is acceptable to the members who prefer B008. If they see it as acceptable, the choice between B035 and B008 is close and I would not oppose B008.
I cannot independently verify the AMANDA and IceCube design history needed to attribute B023, and I defer to an expert report.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B035 or B008 from my profile. My collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) are in astroparticle physics and are adjacent to IceCube (B023), with no named link to Halzen, Karle or Spiering. I would therefore ask the committee to record the field closeness if B023 advances, and I would not lead the argument for it. I have no tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. As Chair I note the disclosures of Johansson (B004, B012), Olsson (B019) and Kroll (Hall/JILA), and none of them, as stated, prevents discussion of B035 or B008.
